narrative:
The model predicted a 60.2% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability exceeded the school's acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three aspects of your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest factor pushing the prediction toward failure. Standing in the bottom decile, far below the average of accepted students (around the middle of the class), signaled to the model a high risk of struggling with the bar. Your first-year ranking had a similar but smaller effect; again placing in the lowest decile rather than near the middle of the class reinforced the same concern.

Your undergraduate GPA of 2.60 worked in the opposite direction. While still below the 3.23 average of accepted students, this feature slightly lowered the predicted risk of failure. However, its positive influence was not strong enough to overcome the impact of your class rankings.

Your family income, LSAT score of 34, full-time study plans, gender, and race played little or no role in the outcome; the model focused almost entirely on your academic performance trajectory.

To improve your chances, you should consider retaking key courses to raise your GPA, seeking structured bar-prep support early, or applying to schools with different admissions thresholds while strengthening the weakest parts of your record.
